title: TailGuard: quantile-driven admission and shape-aware batching
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem summary:
Redwood's continuous batching pipeline reduces average cost but exposes long tail latencies when admission policy mixes large prefill-heavy requests with short, latency-sensitive decodes. Current admission heuristics amplify worst-case wait times for P99+ requests during transient spikes and when kernel scheduling chooses slower paths for mixed-shape batches.

Goals:
- Implement a quantile-driven admission controller (TailGuard) that maintains configurable latency quantiles (P50/P95/P99 targets) per route and tenant while maximizing GPU utilization.
- Introduce a shape-aware batch shaper that groups requests by decode/prefill characteristics and kernel affinity to avoid expensive kernel fallbacks within a single batch.
- Add decode-prefill scheduling hooks so the runtime can preemptively reserve slots for short decodes (latency-sensitive) without regressing throughput for large prefill-heavy workloads.
- Provide observable SLOs and an incremental rollout plan with safe fallbacks to today’s admission logic.

Design highlights and trade-offs:
1) Quantile controller: maintain an exponentially-weighted moving estimate of service times across quantiles per route. Use these estimates to compute an admission score for new arrivals. Admission is probabilistic for low-priority traffic to protect configured quantiles. Trade-off: slight reduction in throughput for higher tail predictability; we will tune via controlled experiments.

2) Shape-aware batching: attach a compact descriptor to each request (prefill_length_bucket, decode_length_bucket, kv_cache_presence, model_variant_hint). During admission, batcher forms batches by preferred-shape buckets but allows limited mixing when utilization is low. This avoids kernel fallback from int8->fp16 or differently tiled kernels. Trade-off: fragmented batches reduce batching elasticity at very low load; mitigated by a fallback window where strict shape enforcement relaxes.

3) Decode reservation: the admission controller reserves a small, dynamic percentage of concurrent decode slots for short-latency requests based on recent arrival rates. Reservation shrinks/grows automatically with observed short-request throughput. Trade-off: potential underutilization during long-prefill-only bursts, but this is bounded by a conservative cap and dynamic reclaim policy.

4) Kernel-affinity hints: integrate with kernel selector so batches carry affinity flags; the runtime can surface costs and expected kernels in trace logs to help tuning. This is read-only hint initially to avoid coupling; later we may allow stronger kernel steering.

Metrics and success criteria:
- P99 latency (decode path) improves by >= 30% in mixed workloads (internal synthetic mix: 20% short decode, 30% medium, 50% long prefill).
- Utilization drop <= 8% vs baseline for the same mix.
- No regression in P50; error rate unchanged.
- Rollout guard triggers (automated rollback) if P99 increases by >10% in production within a rollout window.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0: unit/integration tests + microbenchmarks on canary cluster (dev) with synthetic workload (end of week 1).
- Phase 1: Shadow admission on production with telemetry only (2 weeks).
- Phase 2: Canary enable for 5% traffic with automated rollback monitors (1 week).
- Phase 3: Gradual ramp to 100% with configuration knobs per-tenant and per-route.

Safety and fallbacks:
- Default fallback mode is the existing admission logic. TailGuard only flips live after an explicit runtime feature flag.
- A per-tenant emergency cutoff will immediately revert to baseline if dropped utilization or error spike exceeds thresholds.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Exact bucketing scheme for prefill/decode lengths and whether to encode token-count ranges or raw percentiles.
- Whether kernel-affinity hints should be advisory or enforceable (affects complexity of kernel selector).
- Exact costing model to compute probabilistic admission thresholds (should we use reinforcement-learned thresholds later?).

updates: 2026-02-19: Kickoff meeting with runtime, infra, and observability. Agreed on quantile targets: P95=120ms, P99=240ms for decode routes.
2026-02-23: Prototype of quantile estimator merged to feature branch; microbench harness produces stable estimators on synthetic load.
2026-03-01: Shape descriptor schema finalized (4 prefill buckets x 3 decode buckets + kv flag). Documented in design doc.
2026-03-03: Benchmarks show 35% P99 improvement in dev canary with 10% utilization cost for mixed workloads. Shortlisting tuning parameters.
2026-03-07: Integrated kernel-affinity hint into batch metadata (read-only); kernel selector logging added. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1892
2026-03-10: Shadow rollout configured in prod for two low-risk routes (chatbot-dev, search-sim). Telemetry collection enabled and linked to canary dashboard. Observability owners: Elena Soto.
2026-03-10: Blockers: small race condition observed when reclaiming reserved decode slots under high churn. Assigned to eng: ENG-27611 (follow-up).
